title: Statutes of Limitation by Province
subtitle: Find the right clock before an old debt starts running the meeting

blocks.text: Old debt can arrive in a fresh envelope with the confidence of a brand-new invoice. The law cares less about the envelope than about the timeline.

This course helps you screen an older unsecured consumer debt before you pay, promise or ignore anything. You will separate the court deadline from the credit-report time limit, work out which jurisdiction applies and build a dated evidence file for local advice. The result is a careful next step, not a homemade legal verdict.
A limitation period is usually the time limit to start a court case. It does not automatically erase a debt or remove accurate report information.

items.title: “When a limitation period ends, the debt disappears automatically.”
items.text: Limitation law usually limits a court remedy. It is not a universal debt eraser. The legal effect varies, and Newfoundland and Labrador has its own wording about ending the right.

blocks.text: Meet Jordan
paragraphs: Jordan Chen is a warehouse dispatcher in Halifax. He is about to apply for an apartment and wants no surprises.

Then an email arrives about an old store-card balance. The account has been sold twice, and the amount is bigger than he remembers. The fix sounds tidy: pay $20 today to “show good faith,” or face legal action within forty-eight hours.
Twenty dollars sounds harmless. Instead of sending it, Jordan opens a folder.

In go the agreement, the statements, the last-payment record and an old email where he wrote that he would “try to catch up.” Then he asks the collector, in writing, for the creditor, a breakdown of the balance and the dates.

A community legal clinic tells him the usual time limit is only the start. Where he lived, the type of claim, any acknowledgement and any part payment can all matter. A token payment is not a harmless test.
So Jordan does not declare the debt expired, and he does not ignore it. He keeps every message and avoids admitting he owes it. When a court document does arrive, he gets help and answers on time.
The matter ends with a documented resolution, not the collector’s countdown clock. The $20 never left his account. It bought groceries instead of an accident.

blocks.text: Jordan’s strongest move was the pause between the pressure and the payment. It turned an old account into a dated case file that someone could review.
The conclusion
This does not mean you should never pay an old debt. It means you should not make a legally meaningful move before you understand the clock, the claim and the papers.
You can tell which date governs a lawsuit and which one only governs your credit report.

sections.title: Exhibit A: One Account Can Carry Four Timelines

blocks.text: The most common mistake is treating every date as the same date. Put each clock on its own line.

items.title: COURT-CLAIM LIMITATION
items.text: The deadline to start a civil court case, subject to the law, discovery and exceptions. Which law applies, what is the claim and when could it have been discovered?

items.title: CREDIT-REPORT RETENTION
items.text: How long information may stay under reporting rules and bureau practices. What is the delinquency or reporting date, and is the entry accurate?

items.title: COLLECTION CONDUCT
items.text: How a collector may contact you and which regulator takes complaints. Where do you live, who is collecting and which rules apply?

items.title: JUDGMENT ENFORCEMENT
items.text: How an existing judgment may be enforced. A judgment is not the same as an account nobody has taken to court. Was a claim filed or a judgment entered? Which court, what date and what file number?

blocks.text: A six-year credit-report entry does not create a six-year lawsuit deadline.

items.title: “If an item is gone from my credit report, no one can sue.”
items.text: Report removal and civil limitation law are separate. A missing tradeline does not prove that a claim is barred or that no judgment exists.

blocks.text: THE COURTROOM-DOCUMENT RULE
Never ignore a Statement of Claim or other court document because you believe time has run out.
Limitation may be a defence that has to be raised the right way and on time. Check the court and get help quickly.
FCAC: Credit-report retention
These are the ordinary civil-debt periods, as a screening guide only.

This August 2026 first-pass guide is not a legal conclusion. The claim, the contract, discovery, transition law, acknowledgement, payment, judgment, security or a special statute may change the answer.

items.title: 2 YEARS — Alberta, British Columbia, Manitoba, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Ontario and Saskatchewan
items.text: Modern statutes generally use discovery-based basic periods. Ultimate periods and transition rules may matter.

items.title: 3 YEARS — Quebec and Nunavut
items.text: Quebec generally uses a three-year prescription for a personal action. Nunavut’s 2023 changes use three years after discovery to recover money, with a ten-year ultimate period.

items.title: 6 YEARS — Newfoundland and Labrador, Northwest Territories, Prince Edward Island and Yukon
items.text: Statutes have six-year categories that apply to recovering debt or money. The trigger, any confirmation rules and other wording still need local analysis.

items.title: SPECIAL TRACK — Judgments, secured claims, tax or government debt, student obligations, support orders and other statutory claims
items.text: Do not force these into the ordinary unsecured-debt table. Find the special law and get qualified advice.

blocks.text: Manitoba’s current general period, which runs from discovery, is two years. Nunavut’s period for recovering money changed to three years in 2023. Old charts can be confidently outdated.

items.title: “Canada has one national limitation period for consumer debt.”
items.text: Limitation law is set by each province or territory, and the type of claim and the facts can change the answer.

sections.title: Evidence Hearing: Build the Timeline Before Testing the Clock

blocks.text: Write “unknown” when a fact is missing. A guess dressed as a date is still a guess.
Build the timeline before testing the clock

items.title: Agreement and jurisdiction
items.text: The contract, where the account was opened, any governing-law wording and where you have lived.

items.title: Payment history
items.text: The last payment date and amount, bank proof and the first missed payment that was never made up.

items.title: Default events
items.text: Statements, demand or acceleration notices, account closure and letters.

items.title: Acknowledge­ments
items.text: Any signed or written recognition of the debt, any part payment, the exact words, the date and who made it.

items.title: Assignment history
items.text: The original creditor, any buyers or collectors and the balance breakdown. A sale does not normally restart the clock on its own.

items.title: Court status
items.text: Any claim, service papers, defence, order or judgment. Check the court yourself.

blocks.text: A payment or a qualifying acknowledgement can affect the analysis in many places. The form, the timing and the effect after expiry are not the same everywhere.

items.title: “Selling a debt automatically starts a new limitation period.”
items.text: A transfer changes who is claiming the account. It does not normally create a new default date on its own. Other later events may matter.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: A collector offers a token-payment plan on an eight-year-old account. What should you do before you pay?
items.detail: Save the offer, gather the timeline and get advice for the place that applies before you pay or acknowledge anything.

items.title: Why is credit-report removal not enough to work out the court-claim period?
items.detail: Report retention and civil limitation are separate clocks, with different rules and different dates.

items.title: A court document arrives after you thought the period had expired. What is safest?
items.detail: Check the court, get help right away and file the required response on time. Limitation may need to be raised as a defence.

items.title: Which facts can make a screening period unreliable on its own?
items.detail: The type of claim, the jurisdiction, discovery, transition law, acknowledgement, part payment, judgment, security and special statutes.

items.title: Does a debt sale normally reset the clock on its own?
items.detail: No. A sale changes who claims the account. It does not normally create a new default date by itself.

blocks.text: The word “old” is not a legal date. A useful file holds events, evidence and the law that may apply.

sections.title: Your Action: Prepare Your Limitation Clock Brief

blocks.text: Complete this before you talk to a lawyer, clinic or consumer office. Do not include full account numbers, and do not send it to a caller you have not verified.
A clean timeline lets an adviser spend less time rebuilding the account and more time on the legal question.
A limitation period is a legal clock, not a debt-erasing button.
blocks.detail: Separate the clocks, keep your evidence and get local advice before you pay, acknowledge or ignore an old claim.

items.title: Limitation period
items.text: A time limit set by law for starting a legal case. The law and the facts decide how it applies.

items.title: Discovery
items.text: The point when someone knew, or should reasonably have known, the key facts needed to bring a claim.

items.title: Acknowledgement
items.text: A statement that recognizes a claim or debt. It may affect timing if the law’s requirements are met.

items.title: Part payment
items.text: A payment of less than the full balance. In some places it can affect the limitation analysis.

items.title: Prescription
items.text: The word often used in Quebec for what time does to rights and remedies.

items.title: Judgment
items.text: A court’s formal decision. Enforcing it follows different rules from an account nobody has taken to court.

items.title: Ultimate period
items.text: A longer outside deadline that can apply even if discovery happens later, with some exceptions.
